FOUNDATION
Before we connect sentences
SEE THE PARTS
Sara reads a book.
SUBJECT
Sara = the person who acts.
VERB
reads = the action.
OBJECT
a book = what she reads.
Find the three parts: The students use an app.

What is a clause?
A CLAUSE
A clause normally has a subject and a
verb.
MAIN CLAUSE
The student smiles.
This can stand on its own.
RELATIVE CLAUSE
who helps others
This describes a noun and needs a
main clause.
Find the verb in each example.

Notice the relationship

The student is kind.
She helps her classmates.

Which word in the second sentence
refers to the student?

Look at the student and she.

1 • START
The student is kind.

She helps her classmates.

What does WHO do?
READ THE SENTENCE
The student who helps her
classmates is kind.
MEANING
The relative clause describes the
student.
GRAMMATICAL JOB
Who is the subject of helps. The
student performs the action.
Point to the noun described by WHO.

UNDERSTAND
WHO describes a person
EXAMPLE
The runner who runs is my friend.
LOOK INSIDE
The runner performs the running.
Who refers to the runner and is the
subject of runs.
Which person does WHO refer to?
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy

UNDERSTAND
WHICH describes a thing
EXAMPLE
The app which reminds me to rest
is useful.
LOOK INSIDE
Which refers to the app.
The app performs the reminding.
Think of a useful app. Describe what it does.

UNDERSTAND
THAT can describe a person
EXAMPLE
The student that helped me smiled.
DEFINING CLAUSE
That may replace who here. The
relative clause identifies the student.
Which person does THAT refer to?

UNDERSTAND
THAT can describe a thing
EXAMPLE
The book that I read was useful.
DEFINING CLAUSE
That may replace which here. I read
the book: object role.
The next card shows an important limit.

UNDERSTAND
One limit: extra information
EXAMPLE
My sister, who lives in Cairo, called.
KEEP WHO
This clause adds extra information.
It has commas.
Do not use that in a non-defining
clause.

Who does the action?
COMPLETE
The girl _____ rides her bike is my
friend.
CHOOSE
A. who
B. where
C. whose
Pause. Choose and explain your reason.

PRACTISE • ANSWER
The subject clue
MODEL ANSWER
The girl who rides her bike is my
friend.
WHY WHO?
Girl is a person.
Who is the subject of rides.
WHY NOT THE OTHERS?
Where links a place.
Whose shows possession.

UNDERSTAND
Subject or object?
THE STUDENT ACTS
The student who helps me ...
The student gives the help.
I ACT
The student whom I help ...
I give the help to the student.
EVERYDAY ENGLISH
Who is also commonly used as an
object.
In each example, who performs HELP?

UNDERSTAND
Essential or additional?
DEFINING
Students who revise feel prepared.
The clause identifies WHICH students.
No commas.
NON-DEFINING
Mona, who lives nearby, walks to
school.
Mona is already identified.
The clause adds information: use
commas.

Do commas change meaning?
READ
My sister who lives in Cairo is a doctor.
ASSUME
I have only one sister.
DECIDE
What punctuation is needed? Why?
Pause. Explain before you reveal the clue.

What is already known?
CLUE
If I have only one sister, you already
know which person I mean.
ASK YOURSELF
Does her location identify her, or add
extra information?
Try again before turning the page.

ANALYSE • ANSWER
Commas enclose extra information
MODEL ANSWER
My sister, who lives in Cairo, is a
doctor.
WHY IT WORKS
The extra information has a comma
before and after it.
REMEMBER
Do not use that in this non-defining
clause.
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy
22 / 41

UNDERSTAND
WHOSE links possession
ASK
Whose book? Whose brother? Whose
roof?
RELATIONSHIP
Whose + noun links a possessor to
something or someone related to
them.
COMPARE
Who has a role inside a clause.
Whose connects a possessor to a
noun.
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy
23 / 41

UNDERSTAND
Build with WHOSE
1 • START
Sara is my friend.
2 • SECOND FACT
Her brother studies medicine.
3 • LINK
Her brother means Sara's brother. Use
whose brother.
4 • RESULT
Sara, whose brother studies medicine,
is my friend.
Keep both original facts. Do not invent new
ones.
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy
24 / 41

ANALYSE
WHERE or WHICH?
LOCATION
The museum where we met is old.
We met in the museum.
Here, where = in / at which.
OBJECT
The museum which we visited is old.
We visited the museum.
Visited needs an object.
A place noun alone does not decide the word.
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy

UNDERSTAND
Time, place, possession
WHEN • TIME
The day when we met was special.
We met on that day.
WHERE • PLACE
The room where we study is bright.
We study in that room.
WHOSE • POSSESSION
The student whose bag is red is
here.
The bag belongs to the student.
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy

UNDERSTAND
When may we omit a word?
WITH WHICH
The film which I watched was
interesting.
WITHOUT WHICH
The film I watched was interesting.
WHY?
I is the subject. Which is the object of
watched. An object relative pronoun
can be omitted in a defining clause.
Can you remove WHO from: The girl who won
smiled?

Do not repeat the object
INCORRECT
The film which I watched it was
interesting.
CORRECT
The film which I watched was
interesting.
CAUSE
Which already stands for the object.
Adding it repeats the same object.

PRACTISE • ERROR
Do not delete the subject
INCORRECT
The student won the prize is happy.
CORRECT
The student who won the prize is
happy.
CAUSE
Who is the subject of won inside the
describing clause. It cannot simply
disappear.

I bought the phone.
The relative pronoun is the object.

The woman's son plays football.
Whose son expresses the

3 • WHERE
We met in the park.

FOUNDATION
Meaning before form
CONDITION
One situation that an outcome
depends on.
RESULT
What follows if the condition happens.
CHOOSE THE PERSPECTIVE
Is the situation realistic, imagined, or
in a past we cannot change?
Read the situation first. Choose the form
second.
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy

FOUNDATION
Two connected ideas
READ
If I exercise, I feel better.
SEPARATE THE PARTS
If I exercise = the condition.
I feel better = the result.
GENERAL PATTERN
Present + present describes a regular
pattern here, often called the zero
conditional.
Which part says what needs to happen?
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy

DISCOVER
Imagine an exam week
CONTEXT
A student wants to prepare well.
POSSIBLE ACTION
Studying is something the student can
do.
POSSIBLE CONSEQUENCE
Success may follow. Connect the
action to its consequence.
What condition would help the student
prepare?
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy
06 / 41

UNDERSTAND
A realistic possibility
EXAMPLE
If I study, I will pass.
SPEAKER’S PERSPECTIVE
The speaker treats studying as
possible and predicts a future result.
NOTICE
This is a possible future consequence
in the example.
Point to the condition and the result.
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy
07 / 41

UNDERSTAND
Imagine a different present
EXAMPLE
If I had more time, I would study
more.
SPEAKER’S PERSPECTIVE
The speaker imagines a different
present situation.
NOTICE
The past form can show distance from
reality, rather than past time.
Which part is imagined?

UNDERSTAND
First conditional: possible future
PATTERN
if + present simple
will + base verb
EXAMPLE
If the school offers support, students
will benefit.
MEANING
The condition is treated as realistic.
The result is a possible future
consequence.
Which condition must be satisfied?

1 • MEANING
Studying is possible. Understanding may
follow.
2 • CONDITION
If I study hard, ...
3 • RESULT
... I will understand the lesson.
4 • CHECK
If I study hard, I will understand the
lesson.
Keep the intended condition-result
relationship.

A real future consequence
MODEL ANSWER
If you sleep well, you will feel more
focused tomorrow.
WHY IT WORKS
The condition is presented as a
possible action. Will feel gives its
possible future result.
Which word points to future time?

Second conditional: imagine

Suppose you do not have much free

IMAGINE A CHANGE
Imagine a different present life. What

The past form often signals distance
from reality, not a completed past event.
Describe the reality before imagining the

1 • REALITY
I do not have much free time.
2 • IMAGINE
If I had more free time, ...
3 • RESULT
... I would play sports more often.
4 • MEANING
I am imagining a different present
situation.
Do not confuse a past form with past time.

If I have time, I will visit you.

HYPOTHETICAL
If I had time, I would visit you.
I imagine having time, perhaps
contrary to reality.
Choose the meaning before choosing the
pattern.

Does the speaker have time?
READ
If I had more time, I would join the
team.

Is this presented as a realistic plan or a
hypothetical wish?

page.

Past form, present imagination
MODEL ANSWER
The speaker imagines a different
present situation.
WHY IT WORKS
Had with would join expresses
hypothetical meaning here.
TIME CHECK

action.
What reality might the speaker be imagining
differently?

Third conditional: look back
WHAT HAPPENED
Yesterday, a student missed the bus
and arrived late.
THE PAST IS FIXED
We cannot change that event now.
IMAGINE AN ALTERNATIVE
We can imagine a different past and its
unreal result.
This is reflection on an alternative past, not a
prediction.

UNDERSTAND
Build the third conditional
REAL PAST
IMAGINED PAST
1 • FACT

bus.

Perspective 3: unreal past

See the meaning first
BEFORE CHANGING WORDS
Find who performs the action.
Find who receives the action.

Keep the same meaning when you
change the description.
Meaning must survive every transformation.

Noun, verb, performer, receiver
ACTIVE
A student carries a bag.
PASSIVE
A bag is carried by a student.
FOLLOW THE ACTION
The student performs carrying.
The bag receives the action.
Point to the performer, then the receiver.

Find the right woman
CONTEXT
A woman stands near a temple. Other
people are there too.
YOUR PURPOSE
Identify the woman using a
description.
What information helps your listener find her?

UNDERSTAND
ACTIVE: the noun acts
EXAMPLE
The woman standing near the gate
is a tourist.
MEANING
The woman performs the standing.
FORM
Use an -ing participle for this active
description.
Which noun performs the action?

PASSIVE: the noun receives
EXAMPLE
The bridge built last year is strong.
MEANING
People built the bridge. The bridge
receives the building action.

Built is the past participle of build.
Which noun receives the action?

UNDERSTAND
What is a participle?
PRESENT PARTICIPLE
working
PAST PARTICIPLE
built / written / repaired
FUNCTION
A participle can help describe a noun.
Its form alone does not prove WHEN
the event happened. Context supplies
the time.
Who acts in: students studying together?

The girl performs the reading.
3 • REDUCE
Remove who is. Keep reading.

The girl reading is Mona.
Check that the intended meaning stays the
same.

Find the performer

The noun performs the action
MODEL ANSWER
The students waiting outside are
calm.
WHY IT WORKS
Students perform the waiting.
The -ing phrase identifies WHICH
students.
Point to the noun and its describing phrase.

Shorten a passive description

The report which was written

2 • IDENTIFY
The report receives the action write.
3 • REDUCE
Remove which was. Keep written.
4 • RESULT
The report written yesterday is
clear.
Keep the time information: YESTERDAY.

Who acts? Who receives?

The teacher explaining the rule is
kind.
The teacher explains: -ing.

The rule explained by the teacher is
clear.
The rule receives explanation: past
participle.
Changing the noun changes the action
relationship.

Active action: PLAYING

The children playing outside are

The children perform the playing.

playing outside tells us which

Completed preparation: PREPARED

The food prepared earlier was

Someone prepared the food.
The food receives preparation.

Earlier places the preparation before

Why does PREPARING change the relationship?

Workers are repairing the road now.

ongoing passive action here.
Is the work finished, or still happening?

BEING REPAIRED matters
ONGOING
The bridge being repaired is closed.

COMPLETED

These descriptions have different time

The passive participle

The report written yesterday is
useful.
WHY WRITTEN?
Written is the past participle. It
describes the report as receiving the
action.
WHY NOT WRITING?
Writing would wrongly make the
report perform the writing in this
sentence.

The whole participial phrase

NOT JUST -ING

ITS JOB

Attach the action to its performer

CORRECT

Not every verb becomes -ING

CORRECT
The book written by the author was
helpful.
CAUSE

relationship.
Who writes: the book or the author?
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy

Meaning first, then English
READ
The bridge built last year is strong.
FOLLOW THE SCENE
People built it. The bridge received the
building action.
RETURN TO ENGLISH
Built last year describes the bridge
and keeps the time clue.
Explain the meaning in Arabic, then read it in
English.

Worked example: eating well

People eating well may feel better.
ACTION RELATIONSHIP
People perform the eating.
Use the active -ing phrase.
Name the noun and its describing phrase.

Worked example: a completed project
EXAMPLE
The project completed by our class
won.
ACTION RELATIONSHIP
The class completed the project.
The project receives completion.
FORM
Completed is a past participle.
Why is this a passive description?
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy
29 / 37

PRACTISE
Worked example: ongoing cleaning
EXAMPLE
The hall being cleaned is unavailable.
ACTION RELATIONSHIP
Someone is cleaning the hall now. The

ONGOING PASSIVE
Keep being cleaned to show work in
progress.
What would change if the cleaning were
already finished?
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy

Try two reductions
1 • THE BOY
The boy who is carrying a camera is
Ali.
2 • THE POSTER
The poster which was designed
yesterday is clear.
YOUR TASK
Reduce both relative clauses.
Explain active or passive meaning.
Pause. Try both before revealing the clue.
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy
31 / 37

MASTER • HINT
Choose the action relationship
ASK ABOUT THE NOUN
Does it perform the action, or
receive it?
LOOK AT EACH ACTION
carrying → the boy
designed → the poster
Try again before turning the page.
Prepared by Dr. Mai Abulfotouh  |  Review & Proofreading: Ms. Reham Khafagy

MASTER • ANSWER
Two reductions explained
1 • ACTIVE
The boy carrying a camera is Ali.
The boy performs carrying.
2 • PASSIVE
The poster designed yesterday is
clear.
The poster receives designing.

Keep the noun, action relationship and

Describe a real school scene

Imagine a school exhibition.
Write one sentence about students

Use an active -ing phrase and a

THE SCROLL OF SESHAT
WELCOME TO READ YOUR STORY
A Dream of Adventure
I am Seshat. In ancient Egypt, I was associated with writing, records, 
and knowledge. My image was carved on temple walls, and my 
distinctive emblem appeared above my head.
Today, I open a new scroll for you: A Dream of Adventure. Each 
character will have a special colour and symbol, so you can follow who 
is telling the story and who is speaking.
Come, let the story unfold.

SCENE 01
My name is Edward Malone, and at the time this story began I was a 
young reporter on the Daily Gazette in London.

SCENE 02
I was twenty-three, full of energy, and certain that a great life was 
waiting for me.

SCENE 03
The problem was that I had no idea how to begin it.

SCENE 04
There was also Gladys Hungerton. I admired her more than anyone I had 
ever met, and one evening I finally asked her to marry me.

SCENE 05
She did not laugh at me or become angry. Instead, she looked serious and 
told me that she valued our friendship but did not love me in the way I 
hoped.

SCENE 06
"What kind of man could you love?" I asked. Gladys thought for a moment. "A 
man who has done something brave," she said. "Someone who has faced 
danger, traveled into the unknown, and proved that he can act when it 
matters."

SCENE 07
I tried to joke. "So I must discover a new country before you will 
consider me?"

SCENE 08
"Not for me," she replied. "If a man is truly brave, he does not act just 
to impress someone else. He acts because courage is part of his 
character."

SCENE 09
Her words stayed with me. I left her house feeling disappointed, 
but also strangely excited.

SCENE 10
London suddenly seemed too safe. I wanted a challenge - something that 
would test me and give my life a clearer purpose.

SCENE 11
The next evening I went straight to my editor, Mr McArdle. He was an experienced 
newspaper man who had seen every kind of young reporter. When I asked him to 
send me on a dangerous assignment, he pushed his glasses up and stared at me.

SCENE 12
"You want danger?" he said. "Most sensible people want to avoid it." "I 
want a real story, sir. Something difficult."

SCENE 13
He studied me for a moment, then smiled. "Perhaps I do have a job for you. 
Have you heard of Professor George Edward Challenger?" Of course I had. 
Almost everyone in the newspaper world knew his name.

SCENE 14  ·  1/2
Challenger was a famous zoologist, brilliant but extremely difficult. He had 
recently returned from South America with an extraordinary story about 
unknown animals. When scientists questioned him, he refused to give clear 
details. When reporters tried to interview him, he often threw them out of his 
house - sometimes literally. "Do you want me to interview him?" I asked.

SCENE 14  ·  2/2
"If you can get through the front door," McArdle replied. "Two years ago 
Challenger travelled alone through a little-known part of South America. He 
came back claiming that something remarkable had happened. He had 
damaged photographs, strange sketches, and a few pieces of evidence, but he 
would not reveal the exact place. Most people think he is either mistaken or 
lying. Find out which."

SCENE 15
This was exactly the kind of chance I had been looking for. Yet there was one 
problem: Challenger hated journalists. If I arrived honestly and said I worked for 
the Gazette, the interview would probably end before it began.

SCENE 16
That night I went to the Savage Club, where many writers and scientists met. I 
found my friend Tarp Henry, who worked for a scientific journal, and asked what 
he knew about Challenger.

SCENE 17
"He is clever," Henry said, "but impossible. He argues with everyone. At a 
scientific meeting in Vienna he almost started a battle over a theory of 
evolution. If you want to speak to him, do not mention newspapers."

SCENE 18
That gave me an idea. I asked Henry to find Challenger's latest scientific 
paper. It was full of technical language I barely understood,

SCENE 19
but I copied one complicated sentence and used it in a letter. I pretended to be a 
young student who admired Challenger's work but had a question about one of his 
arguments.

SCENE 20
Henry read the letter and laughed. "You are taking a risk, Malone. He may 
realise at once that you know nothing about the subject." "I only need to get 
inside his study," I said. "After that, I will take my chance."

SCENE 21
Two days later a reply arrived. The handwriting looked as aggressive as the man 
himself. Challenger wrote that my question showed poor understanding, but he 
was willing to explain the matter in person. He gave me an appointment for 
eleven o'clock on Wednesday morning. I should have been nervous. Instead, I felt 
as if my real life had finally begun.

SCENE 22
On Wednesday I traveled to Professor Challenger's large house in 
Kensington.

SCENE 23
A quiet servant named Austin opened the door.

SCENE 24
Before he could take me to the study, a small, lively woman stopped me in 
the hall. "You have come to see my husband?" she asked. "Yes, Mrs 
Challenger."

SCENE 25
She lowered her voice. "Then I should warn you. George is a perfectly 
impossible person. If he becomes angry, do not argue too long. Leave the 
room while you still can." I smiled, but her expression told me she was serious.

SCENE 26
A deep voice suddenly roared from behind a closed door. Austin 
opened it, and I entered.

SCENE 27
Professor Challenger sat behind a wide desk covered with books, maps, fossils, and papers. He 
was shorter than I expected, but enormously broad. His black beard spread across his chest, 
and his sharp grey-blue eyes seemed to measure every weakness in me.

SCENE 28
"Well?" he demanded. "You are the young man who has difficulty 
understanding plain science?" I had entered looking for adventure. I had found 
it sooner than I expected.

Cleopatra VII | The Power of Language and 
Persuasion
I am Cleopatra VII, Queen of Egypt from 51 to 30 BC.
Among the secrets of my power were my command of multiple languages 
and my mastery of the arts of dialogue and persuasion. I made words 
one of my tools of soft power in governance and diplomacy.
That is why I am keen to pass on to you, my descendants, one of the 
secrets of my power: the power of language.
I will take care of you as we review Chapter One of The Lost World: A 
Dream of Adventure. Together, we will revisit its events, discover its 
characters, and test our knowledge through questions and challenges 
that simulate the exam.
Are you ready to take on the challenge with Cleopatra?

"What kind of man could you love?" I 
asked.
"So I must discover a new country before 
you will consider me?"
"I want a real story, sir. Something 
difficult."
"Do you want me to interview him?" I 
asked.
"I only need to get inside his study," I said.
"After that, I will take my chance."
"Yes, Mrs Challenger."

Edward Malone (1/2)
Cleopatra asks
How does disappointment become a new goal?
05
[N] Malone’s narration
My name is Edward Malone, and at the time 
this story began I was a young reporter on the 
Daily Gazette in London.
I was twenty-three, full of energy, and certain 
that a great life was waiting for me.
The problem was that I had no idea how to 
begin it.
There was also Gladys Hungerton. I admired 
her more than anyone I had ever met, and one 
evening I finally asked her to marry me.
I tried to joke.

Her words stayed with me. I left her house 
feeling disappointed, but also strangely 
excited.
London suddenly seemed too safe. I wanted a 
challenge - something that would test me and 
give my life a clearer purpose.

looking for. Yet there was one problem: 
Challenger hated journalists. If I arrived 
honestly and said I worked for the Gazette, the 
interview would probably end before it began.

of technical language I barely understood, but 
I copied one complicated sentence and used it 
in a letter. I pretended to be a young student 
who admired Challenger's work but had a 
question about one of his arguments.
I should have been nervous. Instead, I felt as if 
my real life had finally begun.
